definition: A collection of elements stored in contiguous memory and addressed by index.
wrongs: A chain of nodes in which each element points to the next.
A set of vertices connected by edges that may form cycles.
A last-in first-out sequence with push and pop at one end.
why: The address of element i is the base address plus i times the element size.
example: Thirty exam scores sit in one block so the twelfth score is reached directly by its index.
scenario: A program must read the twelfth daily temperature with a constant-time index into contiguous memory. Which structure fits?
scenarioWhy: An array stores the temperatures contiguously, so index 11 locates the twelfth value directly.

definition: An array that allocates a larger block and copies its elements when capacity is exhausted.
wrongs: An array whose length is fixed when it is created.
A linked chain that never copies elements into a new block.
A complete binary tree stored for priority removal.
why: Most appends are cheap, and the cost of an occasional copy is spread across many insertions.
example: A growable vector doubles from 8 slots to 16 when the ninth item is appended.
scenario: A list backed by an array is full, and the next append allocates a bigger block and copies the old items. What is that list?
scenarioWhy: Growing by allocating and copying is how a dynamic array increases its capacity.

definition: A chain of nodes in which each node stores an element and a link only to the next node.
wrongs: A chain in which each node also stores a link to the previous node.
A contiguous block addressed by index.
A tree in which each node has a left and a right child.
why: Nodes need not be adjacent in memory, and insertion at a known node rewrites a few links.
example: Each song record stores a title and a link to the following song, with no link backward.
scenario: Each song node stores a title and a pointer only to the next song. Which list is that?
scenarioWhy: A single forward link per node is the shape of a singly linked list.

definition: A chain of nodes in which each node links to both the next node and the previous node.
wrongs: A chain whose nodes point only forward.
A structure that inserts and deletes at only one end.
A table that maps keys to slots with a hash function.
why: The backward link lets a known node be removed or lets the chain be walked in reverse without restarting at the head.
example: A history entry points to both a newer page and an older page so either neighbor can be reached directly.
scenario: A known node must be removed by relinking both of its neighbors, using a pointer to the previous node. Which list supports that?
scenarioWhy: The previous pointer lets the neighbors be relinked without scanning from the head.

definition: A sequence in which items are inserted and removed at the same end, called the top.
wrongs: A sequence that removes the item inserted earliest.
A tree that removes the smallest key from the root.
A table that finds a key by hashing it.
why: The last item pushed is the first item popped, which is last-in, first-out order.
example: An editor reverses the most recent text change before it reverses any older change.
scenario: An undo feature must reverse the most recent edit before older edits. Which structure matches that order?
scenarioWhy: Undo pops the latest edit first, which is last-in, first-out behavior.

definition: A sequence that inserts items at the rear and removes them from the front.
wrongs: A sequence that removes the most recently inserted item.
A tree ordered so every left descendant is smaller than the node.
A set that rejects duplicate elements.
why: The earliest item is removed first, which is first-in, first-out order.
example: A printer produces the document that was submitted first while later documents wait behind it.
scenario: People who reach a help desk first should be served first. Which structure models that line?
scenarioWhy: Serving the earliest arrival first is first-in, first-out removal from a queue.

definition: A queue in a fixed array whose front and rear indexes wrap back to the first slot.
wrongs: A queue that only moves forward and never reuses earlier slots.
A stack stored in an array with one top index.
A linked tree with no fixed capacity.
why: Wrapping reuses empty slots at the beginning after removals, without sliding the remaining items down.
example: An eight-slot keyboard buffer stores the next key at index 0 after index 7 has been used.
scenario: A fixed array buffer should reuse freed slots at the front without sliding every remaining element. Which queue layout does that?
scenarioWrongs: A linear queue that never wraps
scenarioWhy: Front and rear wrap to the start of the array, so freed slots are reused in place.

definition: A double-ended queue that allows insertion and removal at both the front and the rear.
wrongs: A sequence that inserts and removes at only one end.
A heap that removes the best priority from the root.
A list whose nodes point only to the next node.
why: Either end can act as the insertion or removal point, so it can behave as a stack or as a queue.
example: A history buffer adds a new page at the front and drops the oldest page from the rear when it is full.
scenario: A scheduler must add urgent jobs at the front of a line and ordinary jobs at the rear. Which structure allows both ends?
scenarioWhy: A deque supports insertion at either end, so urgent and ordinary jobs can enter at different ends.

definition: A tree in which every node has at most two children, usually called left and right.
wrongs: A tree that allows any number of children per node.
A graph that may contain a cycle.
A hash table with one slot per bucket.
why: The two-child limit is the shape used by search trees, heaps, and expression trees.
example: An expression stores plus at the root, with the left child 2 and the right child 3.
scenario: An expression node stores an operator and at most one left operand and one right operand. What kind of tree is that?
scenarioWhy: A node with at most two children is a binary-tree node.

definition: A binary tree in which every key in the left subtree is smaller and every key in the right subtree is larger.
wrongs: A complete tree in which each parent is only ordered against its children.
A graph traversal that visits vertices level by level.
A balanced tree defined only by subtree height, with no key order.
why: Search, insertion, and deletion each follow one path from the root using that order.
example: Looking for 42 goes left when the current key is larger than 42 and right when it is smaller.
scenario: Keys must be found by going left for a smaller key and right for a larger key, starting at the root. Which tree is organized that way?
scenarioWhy: Left-smaller and right-larger ordering is the search property of a binary search tree.

definition: A binary search tree kept balanced so the heights of every node's two subtrees differ by at most one.
wrongs: A binary search tree that may become a straight line after sorted insertions.
A heap that is complete but is not a search tree.
A linked list of keys in insertion order.
why: Rotations after insertion or deletion restore the balance factor, so the height stays logarithmic.
example: Inserting keys in sorted order still triggers rotations so the search tree does not degenerate into a line.
scenario: Insertions arrive already sorted, but the search tree must rotate to keep the two subtree heights within one. Which tree does that?
scenarioWhy: AVL trees restore a height difference of at most one with rotations after each update.

definition: A complete binary tree in which each node is ordered relative to its children, usually stored in an array.
wrongs: A binary tree ordered so the left subtree holds smaller keys and the right holds larger keys.
A linked list ordered by insertion time.
A hash table ordered by hash code.
why: The heap order puts an extreme value at the root, and sifting repairs the tree after that value is removed.
example: Job priorities sit in a complete tree array with the most urgent priority stored at the first index.
scenario: Priorities occupy a complete binary tree in which each parent is ordered against its children and the extreme value is at the root. What is that tree?
scenarioWhy: A complete tree with the parent-child order, and the extreme at the root, is a heap.

definition: A heap in which every parent is less than or equal to its children, so the smallest key is at the root.
wrongs: A heap whose root holds the largest key.
A search tree whose in-order walk is sorted.
A queue that removes items in arrival order.
why: Removing the root takes the minimum, and sifting the last element down restores the parent-child order.
example: A shortest-path computation repeatedly removes the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance from the root.
scenario: A scheduler must repeatedly remove the job with the smallest remaining time from a complete tree. Which heap fits?
scenarioWhy: A min-heap keeps the smallest remaining time at the root for the next removal.

definition: An abstract collection that removes the element with the best priority rather than the oldest element.
wrongs: A line that always removes the element that arrived first.
A sequence that always removes the element inserted last.
A set that only tests whether an element is present.
why: A heap is the usual implementation because it finds the extreme priority in logarithmic time.
example: An emergency room next admits the most urgent patient, not the patient who arrived earliest.
scenario: Patients should be treated by urgency, so the next removal is the most urgent case rather than the earliest arrival. Which abstract structure is that?
scenarioWhy: Removal follows priority rather than arrival time, which is a priority queue.

definition: A structure that maps each key to a slot by computing a hash function on the key.
wrongs: A sorted array searched by repeatedly discarding half of the remaining range.
A stack of keys with no lookup by value.
A queue of keys served in arrival order.
why: A good hash function spreads keys so search, insertion, and deletion take constant time on average.
example: A compiler finds a variable's type from its name without scanning every declared name.
scenario: A compiler must find a variable's type from its name in expected constant time. Which structure fits?
scenarioWhy: Hashing the name selects a slot, giving expected constant-time lookup.

definition: The event that two different keys produce the same hash-table slot.
wrongs: A tree rotation that restores balance after an insertion.
A graph path that returns to its starting vertex.
An array index that falls outside the allocated block.
why: A hash function has a finite range, so unequal keys can land in one bucket and need a resolution method.
example: In a table of 16 slots, the distinct names cat and act both compute bucket 4.
scenario: Two different usernames compute the same index in a table of 16 slots. What is that event called?
scenarioWrongs: An overflow of the array bounds
scenarioWhy: Unequal keys that hash to one slot have collided.

definition: Collision handling that stores every key hashing to one slot in a linked list at that slot.
wrongs: A probe that stores colliding keys in later slots of the table array itself.
A second hash function used to choose the next table slot.
A directory of buckets that splits when a bucket overflows.
why: Only the list at the chosen bucket is scanned, and that list grows as more keys collide there.
example: Bucket 4 holds a short linked list containing both cat and act.
scenario: Keys that hash to the same index should hang in a linked list from that bucket. Which collision method is that?
scenarioWhy: A linked list at the bucket is separate chaining.

definition: Collision handling that stores every key in the table array and probes other slots when a slot is taken.
wrongs: Storage of colliding keys in a linked list outside the slot.
A binary search tree built inside each bucket.
A sorted array that ignores hash codes.
why: There is no bucket list; a probe sequence looks through the array for an empty slot.
example: When slot 4 is occupied, the next attempt tries slot 5 and then slot 6 until an empty slot appears.
scenario: A hash table has no per-bucket lists, and a key that hits a full slot tries later slots in the array. Which collision family is that?
scenarioWrongs: A binary search tree of keys
scenarioWhy: Probing other array slots for an empty place is open addressing.

definition: A set of vertices connected by edges, which may be directed or weighted and may contain cycles.
wrongs: A hierarchical structure in which each node has one parent.
A last-in first-out sequence.
A first-in first-out sequence.
why: Edges can express arbitrary connections, including more than one parent and paths that loop.
example: Campus buildings are vertices, and the walkways between them are edges labeled with walking times.
scenario: Buildings and the walkways between them must be modeled, including routes that loop. Which structure allows those cycles?
scenarioWhy: A graph can contain cycles, which a tree by definition cannot.

definition: A graph representation in which each vertex stores a list of the vertices it is connected to.
wrongs: A two-dimensional array with one entry for every possible pair of vertices.
A matrix that records which vertices lie on which edges in a different layout.
A parent array used only for a tree.
why: The space used is proportional to the number of vertices plus the number of edges, which suits a sparse graph.
example: Person A stores only the friends B and C, not a flag for every other person in a large network.
scenario: A social network is sparse, and each person should store only the people they are linked to. Which representation fits?
scenarioWrongs: A distance matrix of all pairs
scenarioWhy: Each vertex's list holds only its existing edges, which is an adjacency list.

definition: A two-dimensional array in which an entry shows whether an edge joins a particular pair of vertices.
wrongs: A list, per vertex, of only the vertices that share an edge.
A stack of edges in the order they were discovered.
A parent pointer for each vertex in a traversal.
why: Testing one possible edge takes constant time, while the space grows with the square of the vertex count.
example: An entry at row 2 and column 5 equals 1 when a road runs from city 2 to city 5.
scenario: A dense road network needs a constant-time test for whether one specific pair of cities has a road. Which representation fits?
scenarioWhy: One matrix cell answers whether that pair of cities is connected.

definition: A graph traversal that visits vertices in order of increasing distance, in edges, from a start vertex.
wrongs: A traversal that follows one path as far as possible before backtracking.
A shortest-path algorithm for graphs with nonnegative weights.
A walk that visits a tree node before either of its children.
why: A queue explores every neighbor at the current distance before vertices that are farther away.
example: From a maze entrance, rooms one corridor away are listed before rooms two corridors away.
scenario: A maze solver must visit rooms in order of fewest corridors from the entrance, using a queue. Which traversal is that?
scenarioWhy: A queue visits vertices level by level, which is breadth-first search on an unweighted maze.

definition: A graph traversal that follows one path as far as it can before backtracking to try another.
wrongs: A traversal that visits all nearer vertices before farther ones.
A level-order walk of a tree using a queue.
An algorithm that settles the closest weighted vertex next.
why: Recursion or an explicit stack finishes one neighbor's entire path before the next neighbor of the same vertex.
example: A maze walk continues down one corridor to a dead end, then returns to try the next turn.
scenario: A maze solver follows one path to a dead end and then backtracks, using recursion. Which traversal is that?
scenarioWhy: Going as far as possible and then backtracking is depth-first search.

definition: An algorithm for shortest paths from one source when every edge weight is nonnegative.
wrongs: A traversal that counts unweighted hops with a queue.
A traversal that backtracks along one path.
A sort that repeatedly extracts a heap root into an array.
why: It settles the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance and then relaxes that vertex's outgoing edges.
example: A navigation tool computes the smallest total driving time from campus to every junction when road times are nonnegative.
scenario: Road times are nonnegative, and an app needs the shortest time from campus to every other junction. Which algorithm fits?
scenarioWhy: Dijkstra's algorithm computes single-source shortest paths when weights are nonnegative.

definition: An ordering of a directed acyclic graph in which every edge points from an earlier vertex to a later one.
wrongs: A minimum set of edges that connects every vertex with no cycles.
A path of smallest total weight between two vertices.
A level-order listing produced by a queue.
why: Such an order exists only when the directed graph has no cycle, and it places prerequisites first.
example: A course plan lists the introductory course before the course that requires it.
scenario: Courses have prerequisite edges and no cycle. An ordering must place each prerequisite earlier than the course that needs it. What is that ordering?
scenarioWhy: An order that respects every prerequisite edge is a topological sort of the course graph.

definition: A subset of a connected graph's edges that links every vertex with the smallest total weight and no cycle.
wrongs: A path of least weight from one chosen source to the other vertices.
An order of vertices that respects directed prerequisite edges.
A cycle that visits every vertex exactly once.
why: Algorithms such as Kruskal's and Prim's grow an acyclic connection of minimum total cost.
example: The cheapest cables that connect every campus building, without a redundant loop, are selected.
scenario: A campus must connect every building with cable of minimum total cost and with no redundant loop. What should be computed?
scenarioWrongs: A shortest path from one building
scenarioWhy: A minimum spanning tree connects all buildings at the least total cable cost without cycles.

definition: An asymptotic upper bound on how a function grows, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms.
wrongs: A tight bound that is both an upper and a lower bound.
A lower bound that says growth is at least some rate.
A count of the exact number of machine cycles on one CPU.
why: It classifies algorithms by how their cost grows with input size in the worst case commonly considered.
example: A single pass over n exam scores is described as linear even though each score update does a few constant steps.
scenario: A lecturer ignores constant factors and says one pass over n items grows linearly. Which notation records that upper bound?
scenarioWhy: Big-O states an upper bound such as linear growth, dropping constants and lower-order terms.

definition: How the number of basic steps an algorithm performs grows as the input size grows.
wrongs: How the extra memory an algorithm uses grows with the input size.
Whether equal elements keep their original relative order.
The physical cache-line size of one processor.
why: Counting dominant operations compares algorithms without depending on one machine's clock speed.
example: Finding a score in a sorted list by halving the range does a logarithmic number of comparisons.
scenario: Two sorting programs are compared by how their comparison counts grow with n, not by one laptop's timer. What is being compared?
scenarioWhy: Growth in the number of comparisons is time complexity.

definition: How the extra memory an algorithm needs grows as the input size grows.
wrongs: How the number of computational steps grows with the input.
Whether a sort keeps equal items in their original order.
The ratio of stored keys to hash-table slots.
why: It counts auxiliary storage, such as another array or a recursion stack, often separately from the input itself.
example: Combining sorted halves uses a second array as large as the input, so the extra memory grows linearly.
scenario: An algorithm allocates a second array as large as its input, and that extra memory grows with n. What is that growth called?
scenarioWhy: Growth of auxiliary memory with n is space complexity.

definition: A sort that repeatedly swaps adjacent elements that are out of order.
wrongs: A sort that merges two already sorted halves.
A sort that partitions elements around a chosen pivot.
A sort that builds a heap and repeatedly extracts the root.
why: Each pass moves one more extreme element to its end by swapping it with its neighbors.
example: On the list 3, 1, 2, the value 3 swaps with 1 and then with 2 so it reaches the end on the first pass.
scenario: A student sorts a list only by swapping neighbors that are out of order, pass after pass. Which sort is that?
scenarioWhy: Swapping out-of-order neighbors on each pass is bubble sort.

definition: A sort that repeatedly selects the smallest remaining element and swaps it into the next position.
wrongs: A sort that inserts each new element into an already sorted prefix.
A sort that swaps only adjacent out-of-order pairs.
A sort that partitions around a pivot.
why: After i selections, the first i positions hold the i smallest elements in order.
example: On 4, 1, 3, the smallest value 1 is swapped into the first position, then 3 is swapped into the next.
scenario: Each pass finds the smallest not-yet-placed element and swaps it into the next fixed position. Which sort is that?
scenarioWhy: Selecting the minimum of the unsorted suffix and placing it next is selection sort.

definition: A sort that places each next element into its position within the already sorted prefix.
wrongs: A sort that selects the minimum of the unsorted part on each pass.
A sort that extracts successive roots from a heap.
A sort that merges sorted runs from a split array.
why: Larger elements in the sorted prefix shift right until the gap for the new element is found.
example: A card player slides a newly drawn 2 into its place among cards that are already in order.
scenario: A hand of cards is kept in order by sliding each newly drawn card into place among the cards already held. Which sort matches that?
scenarioWhy: Inserting the next item into a sorted prefix is insertion sort.

definition: A divide-and-conquer sort that splits the array, sorts the halves, and then merges those sorted halves.
wrongs: A sort that partitions around a pivot and recurses on the two sides.
A sort that slides each item into a sorted prefix.
A sort that repeatedly swaps adjacent items.
why: Merging two sorted halves takes linear work, and the recurrence solves to linearithmic time.
example: The list 4, 1, 3, 2 is split into halves, each half is sorted, and the halves are then combined into order.
scenario: An array is split until single elements remain, and sorted halves are then combined back into order. Which sort is that?
scenarioWhy: Splitting, sorting the halves, and merging them is merge sort.

definition: A divide-and-conquer sort that partitions elements around a pivot and recursively sorts each side.
wrongs: A sort that merges two sorted halves after a balanced split.
A sort that builds a heap and extracts the root repeatedly.
A sort that bubbles extreme values to the end by adjacent swaps.
why: After partitioning, elements smaller than the pivot are on one side and larger elements are on the other.
example: Choosing 3 as the pivot rearranges a list so smaller values sit to its left and larger values sit to its right.
scenario: A sort chooses a pivot, places smaller elements to its left and larger ones to its right, then repeats on each side. Which sort is that?
scenarioWhy: Partitioning around a pivot and recursing on both sides is quick sort.

definition: A sort that turns the array into a heap and then repeatedly moves the root into the sorted end.
wrongs: A sort that merges sorted halves.
A sort that partitions around a pivot.
A sort that inserts each item into a sorted prefix.
why: Each of the n extractions takes logarithmic time, and only a constant amount of extra memory is required.
example: An array is arranged so the largest value is at the root, and that root is then swapped into the last position.
scenario: A sort first makes the array a max-heap, then repeatedly moves the root to the end and repairs the heap. Which sort is that?
scenarioWhy: Building a heap and extracting the root into the sorted suffix is heap sort.

definition: A search on a sorted array that discards the half of the range that cannot contain the key.
wrongs: A search that checks each element from the start until the key appears.
A graph walk that uses a stack.
A lookup that computes a hash slot from the key.
why: Comparing against the middle element halves the remaining range, so the search is logarithmic.
example: Looking for 8 in the sorted scores 1, 3, 8, 9 compares with the middle and then looks only to the right.
scenario: A sorted score array is searched by comparing with the middle element and ignoring one half each time. Which search is that?
scenarioWhy: Halving a sorted range at each comparison is binary search.

definition: A search that inspects elements one by one until the key is found or the collection ends.
wrongs: A search that halves a sorted range at every comparison.
A search that estimates the key's position from its value.
A graph traversal that visits vertices by increasing distance.
why: Without sorted order or hashing, every element may have to be examined, so the worst case is proportional to the length.
example: Finding the name Mei in an unsorted attendance sheet checks each name from the first row onward.
scenario: Names are unsorted, so a lookup checks the first name, then the next, until it finds a match or finishes the sheet. Which search is that?
scenarioWhy: Checking elements in order from the start is linear search.

definition: A technique in which a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller instance.
wrongs: A single loop that updates one index until a condition fails.
A table that stores answers to overlapping subproblems.
A hash computation used for lookup.
why: Each call must move toward a base case that returns an answer without another call.
example: Computing 5 factorial calls the same function on 4, continuing down until the call on 0 returns 1.
scenario: A function computes n factorial by calling itself on n minus 1 until it reaches 0. What technique is that?
scenarioWhy: The function calls itself on a smaller n until a base case, which is recursion.

definition: A strategy that splits a problem into subproblems, solves them, and combines their answers.
wrongs: A strategy that repeatedly takes the locally best choice and never revises it.
A strategy that stores answers to overlapping subproblems in a table.
A strategy that tries every possible subset.
why: The split reduces the input size, and the combine step produces the answer for the original input.
example: A sort divides an array into two halves, sorts each half, and then merges the sorted halves.
scenario: A problem is split into independent halves, each half is solved, and the two answers are combined. Which strategy is that?
scenarioWhy: Splitting into subproblems and combining their results is divide and conquer.

definition: A strategy that solves each overlapping subproblem once and reuses the stored answer.
wrongs: A strategy that splits independent subproblems and combines them without reuse.
A strategy that always commits to the locally best next choice.
A search that undoes a choice as soon as it fails.
why: A table or memo turns repeated recursive work into a polynomial computation when subproblems overlap.
example: A Fibonacci table fills each entry from the two preceding entries so each value is computed once.
scenario: A recursive Fibonacci routine recomputes the same smaller values many times, so each result is stored in a table. Which strategy is that?
scenarioWhy: Storing and reusing overlapping Fibonacci results is dynamic programming.

definition: An algorithm that builds a solution by repeatedly taking the locally best option and never revising it.
wrongs: An algorithm that fills a table of overlapping subproblems.
An algorithm that splits the input and combines independent answers.
An algorithm that tries every candidate and keeps the best complete one.
why: The choice is final when it is made, and it is correct only for problems with the greedy-choice property.
example: Making change repeatedly takes the largest coin that does not exceed the amount still owed.
scenario: Coin change repeatedly picks the largest coin that does not exceed the remaining amount and never takes that pick back. Which approach is that?
scenarioWhy: Irrevocable locally best choices are the greedy approach.

definition: A sort that preserves the original relative order of elements that compare as equal.
wrongs: A sort that uses only a constant amount of extra memory.
A sort that runs faster when the input is already nearly ordered.
A sort that randomly shuffles equal elements.
why: Stability matters when a later key must not scramble an order already established by an earlier key.
example: Students already ordered by name keep Ada before Ben after a grade sort when Ada and Ben share a grade and Ada was first.
scenario: Students are already ordered by name, and a later sort by grade must keep Ada before Ben when their grades are equal. Which property is required?
scenarioWhy: Stability keeps the earlier name order of students whose grades compare equal.

definition: A binary-tree walk that visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree.
wrongs: A walk that visits the node before either subtree.
A walk that visits both subtrees before the node.
A walk that visits nodes level by level using a queue.
why: On a binary search tree, this order visits the keys from smallest to largest.
example: A search tree with root 4, left child 2, and right child 6 yields 2, then 4, then 6.
scenario: A search tree should be printed from the smallest key to the largest by visiting left, node, then right. Which traversal is that?
scenarioWhy: Left, node, then right visits binary-search-tree keys in sorted order.

definition: A binary-tree walk that visits the node, then the left subtree, then the right subtree.
wrongs: A walk that visits the left subtree before the node.
A walk that visits the node only after both subtrees.
A walk that visits a tree level by level.
why: The node is processed before its children, matching a prefix listing of an expression tree.
example: An expression tree rooted at plus with children 2 and 3 yields plus, then 2, then 3.
scenario: An expression tree should list the operator before its operands by visiting the node first. Which traversal is that?
scenarioWhy: Visiting the node before its children lists the operator first.

definition: A binary-tree walk that visits the left subtree, then the right subtree, then the node.
wrongs: A walk that visits the node before its children.
A walk that visits the node between the two subtrees.
A walk that uses a queue to visit level by level.
why: Children are processed before their parent, which suits deleting a tree or evaluating an expression.
example: An expression tree rooted at plus with children 2 and 3 yields 2, then 3, then plus.
scenario: A tree should be freed by releasing both subtrees before releasing the node itself. Which traversal order matches that?
scenarioWhy: Post-order visits both children before the node, so subtrees can be freed first.

definition: The ratio of the number of stored keys to the number of slots in a hash table.
wrongs: The height difference of the two subtrees of a tree node.
The maximum number of children a tree node may have.
The depth of the deepest leaf in a heap.
why: A high ratio means more collisions, so tables often resize after the ratio passes a threshold.
example: A table with 8 slots and 6 keys has a ratio of 0.75, a common point at which the table grows.
scenario: A hash table holds 6 keys in 8 slots and resizes when that ratio passes 0.75. What is the ratio called?
scenarioWhy: Keys divided by slots is the load factor that triggers resizing.

definition: An average of operation costs over a sequence, so an occasional expensive step is spread across cheaper ones.
wrongs: A bound on the single most expensive call, considered alone.
A bound that assumes the luckiest possible input.
An average that assumes random pivot choices inside one sort.
why: A costly resize can be charged across the many cheap insertions that filled the previous capacity.
example: One append copies every item in a doubling array, yet across a long series of appends the average cost per append stays constant.
scenario: One append copies n items, but over a long series of appends the average cost per append stays constant. What kind of analysis shows that?
scenarioWhy: Averaging the rare copy across many cheap appends is amortized analysis.

definition: A search that builds a candidate step by step and abandons it as soon as it cannot succeed.
wrongs: A search that always keeps the locally best choice.
A table method that reuses overlapping subproblems.
A hash lookup that jumps directly to a slot.
why: The latest choice is undone and the next alternative is tried, so failed branches are not kept.
example: A puzzle solver places a digit, finds the row illegal, removes that digit, and tries the next digit.
scenario: A puzzle solver places a digit, discovers the row is illegal, removes that digit, and tries another. Which technique is that?
scenarioWhy: Undoing a failing choice and trying the next one is backtracking.

definition: A path in a graph that begins and ends at the same vertex.
wrongs: A path that visits every vertex exactly once and does not return.
A set of edges that connects every vertex without repeating a vertex.
An order of vertices that respects every directed edge.
why: A directed cycle means no topological order exists, and a cycle means a connected graph is not a tree.
example: Prerequisite links from A to B, B to C, and C back to A loop, so those courses cannot be ordered.
scenario: Prerequisites say A before B, B before C, and C before A. Why can no valid course order exist?
scenarioWhy: The three prerequisite edges form a cycle, and a cycle cannot be topologically ordered.

definition: A path between two vertices whose total edge weight is the smallest among all such paths.
wrongs: A set of edges that connects every vertex at minimum total cost.
An order of vertices that respects directed prerequisites.
A path that visits every vertex exactly once.
why: Unweighted graphs can use breadth-first search, while nonnegative weights call for Dijkstra's algorithm.
example: Among several campus routes from the library to the lab, the route whose times add to 6 minutes is the smallest total.
scenario: Several routes connect the library to the lab, and an app must report the route whose travel times add to the smallest total. What is that route?
scenarioWhy: The route with the smallest total travel time between those two places is a shortest path.
